title: Lack of trained staff hampered council's response to Wellington extreme flooding - officials
text:
Lack of trained staff hampered council's response to Wellington extreme flooding - officials
Officials at Wellington City Council say a lack of trained staff compromised its response to extreme flooding and they're warning there's not enough skilled people to handle a bigger disaster.
During the 20 April flash flooding, staff competence varied, public communication on the emergency was lacking, and some flood victims' needs fell through the cracks, the Civil Defence controller told councillors on Tuesday.
A state of emergency was declared in Wellington on 20 April as torrential rain, flooding and slips caused extensive damage to people's homes, property and businesses.
More than one hundred homes in the capital were affected - with 35 homes needing emergency accommodation support, and more than one hundred applying for rates relief.
One man, Phillip Sutton, died after he was swept away in floodwaters from his South Karori home.
Over 89 millimetres of rain was recorded in one hour in Berhampore, councillors heard, the equivalent of a one in 250 year storm.
Phil Becker, emergency management and city development manager, said at a briefing on Tuesday there wasn't enough trained emergency operation centre staff as the weather hit, and it was "very difficult" to get enough people.
"The capability at some of the staff level is very variable - there is some strong capability in some areas, and not-so-strong in other areas."
Becker admitted that communication to both the public and councillors during the emergency was "left wanting".
"There was good effort there, but the quality of the information, we thought, could be better...and reducing the ambiguity that landed with yourselves as councillors at times."
Emergency staff didn't "identify the immediate needs of people on the ground - particularly in those early days".
"So we were caught short there."
Becker said the experience level of staff was "under-strength" for a larger, longer emergency.
He said the emergency operations centre was set up quickly, and staff were focused on identifying risks, with information improving once people "knew what was going on".
Council executives had committed to an "improvement programme", Becker said, with two internal reviews done.
"We are our own harshest critics ... the team are very aware of the obligation they carry in serving the city. We don't not turn over rocks and look for improvements."
Southern ward councillor Laurie Foon said many people felt abandoned as floodwaters swept through their homes, and they were unable to reach emergency services.
Others tried to call the council but were finding that call-takers - some located in Palmerston North - had "no idea what was happening", she said.
Becker replied that he was trying to improve the contact centre's systems.
Fire crews and police were "overwhelmed" and "beyond capacity", he said. "I don't think we would be able to turn out enough people in trucks to pull people out of floodwaters - because that was literally what was happening on the ground."
Officials also described a dangerous slip and flooding that occurred at the dump in Ōwhiro Bay.
One thousand cubic metres of rock had slid into a culvert near Carey's Gully Tunnel at the Southern Landfill - which took two teams three days of non-stop work to empty, waste manager Beth Keightley said.
A culvert at the privately operated C&D landfill also flooded with 60,000 cubic metres of water - forming a lake which was 15 metres deep, 40 metres wide, and 100 metres long.
"That really was a point of quite a lot of concern for the landfill team. Primarily if that water had breached ... the lake, and what that could have meant," Keightley said.
Speaking after the meeting, Wellington mayor Andrew Little told RNZ the April flood had tested the council.
"You can't have a team on standby when the events are unpredictable and infrequent, what you do want to know is that there are staff that have capabilities that can be turned to when the need arises.
"It's now a question of getting on and making sure those improvements happen."

title: Weather: Heavy rain falls on lower North, upper South Island
text:
Weather: Heavy rain falls on lower North, upper South Island
State Highway 6 has reopened between Murchison and Kawatiri Junction in the South Island after being closed because of slips and flooding.
SH65 remains closed between O'Sullivans and Springs Junction because of a slip at Shenandoah.
The New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) says the highway might stay closed Monday night.
SH6 was still closed between Makarora and Lake Hawea because of a slip.
SH67 between Hector and Mokihinui on the West Coast has reopened to a single lane.
NZTA said road users were advised to delay their journeys if possible.
The Tararua Ranges has had almost 100mm of rain over the past 12 hours and will remain under an orange level rain warning until Monday afternoon.
Rain watches also remained in place for parts of Wellington, Waiarapa, Manawatū and Taranaki.
Further south, highways around Nelson and Buller were also closed to flooding and slips.
"Snow is forecast to affect some of the higher-level roads and passes across the South Island," MetService said.
A snowfall warning was in place on the Lewis Pass till at least 9am.
MetService said by Tuesday, there would be minimal risk of severe weather.
"A complex low pressure system moves away to the east of New Zealand as a ridge of high pressure builds over the country. A weak front decays as it moves onto southern New Zealand."
Strong winds were possible by the end of the working week in the southernmost parts of the country.

images.caption: State Highway Six is closed flooding. Photo credit: NZTA/Screenshot
State Highway Six is still closed between Makarora and Lake Hāwea after recent slips. NZTA/Screenshot

title: Weather: Rain and snow warnings issued as trough crosses central NZ
text:
Weather: Rain and snow warnings issued as trough crosses central NZ
Heavy rain is causing flooding, slips and fallen trees across parts of Canterbury and the West Coast.
State Highway 6 between Punakaiki and Fox River was closed closed because of a slip at Meybille Bay, but had since partially reopened.
NZTA Waka Kotahi said flooding was also occurring on several highways between Greymouth, Reefton and Murchison.
Snow was also affecting higher parts of the South Island, including Lindis Pass, with people urged to take extra care on the roads.
Up to 200 millimetres of rain was expected in the ranges today.
MetService said a large trough is crossing central New Zealand on Sunday and early Monday, bringing heavy rain and potentially snow to mountain passes.
An orange-level warning is in place for Grey and Buller Districts, and Nelson Lakes, from 9am Sunday until 1am Monday.
The MetService warning issued at 9:17am said residents should expect "a further 100 to 140 mm of rain about the ranges on top of what has already fallen," and 50-70 mm elsewhere.
It said peak intensities of up to 25mm/h were expected this afternoon and early evening.
At the same time, it issued a heavy rain warning for the Tararua Range, effective from 5pm Sunday until 3pm Monday, with up to 150 millimetres expected overnight.
It said there was a "minimal chance" of the either warning being upgraded, but urged people to avoid low-lying areas.
"Streams and rivers may rise rapidly. Surface flooding, slips, and difficult driving conditions possible."
Rain watches were in place for the Westland ranges north of Mt Cook until 10pm, Tasman west of Takaka until 3am Monday, and the Canterbury High Country north of Mt Cook and southwestern Marlborough until 4am Monday.
Watches will come into force for northern Taranaki at 6pm, southern and eastern Wellington and Wairarapa away from the ranges at 11pm, and the Ruahine Range at 3am Monday.
Road snowfall warnings
By 10am Sunday, MetService had issued road snowfall warnings for five mountain passes in the South Island.
Further north, rain is expected to turn to snow about the summits of Arthur's Pass and Porters Pass (both SH73) from 9pm Sunday until early Monday morning.
And on Lewis Pass (SH7), rain is expected to turn to snow about the summit early on Monday and 2-3cm of snow may accumulate.

images.caption: State Highway 6 closure between Fox River and Punakaiki. Photo credit: Supplied / NZTA Waka Kotahi
MetService's website shows locations covered by warnings and watches at 11am Sunday. MetService / Screenshot

title: Weather: Wind warning in place for Wellington, heavy rain for the South Island
text:
A strong wind warning is in place for the capital on Friday, while parts of the central and northern South Island are being drenched with heavy rain.
MetService said a front impacting parts of the South Island and the Tararua Range had hit on Friday and strong northwesterlies could reach a severe gale in eastern areas from Canterbury all the way up to Hawke's Bay.
Drivers in Canterbury and the West Coast are being warned to expect delays as rain and strong winds hit the regions.
MetService has forecast severe westerly gales reaching 90km/h near Arthur's Pass.
State Highway 7 is down to a single lane with stop/go traffic management in place because of fallen trees near Heslop Creek Bridge, between Rahu Saddle and Springs Junction.
An area warning for slips and flooding is in place on State Highway 73 from Arthur's Pass to Kumara Junction.
MetService has also issued a strong wind watch for the Canterbury high country from 11am until 9pm on Saturday.
It said the winds could approach severe gales in some areas.
Wind gusts of 137km/h on Remutaka hill
A strong wind warning has been issued for Wellington and Wairarapa, excluding the Tararua District, from 4am on Friday through to 12pm.
Severe gales gusting up to 120km/h in exposed places were possible, the forecaster said. This could bring damage to trees, powerlines and unsecured structures and make driving difficult for high-sided vehicles and motorcycles.
Wellington was the windest place overnight - but the warmest at the same time.
MetService meteorologist Braydon White said gusts reached 137km/h at the Remutaka Summit around 7am.
Mount Kaukau followed closely at 136km/h gusts.
Urban areas also saw high winds, with the suburb of Kelburn getting gusts as high as 120km/h.
"We're well into the classic Spring westerlies," White said.
While he said these winds were normal for the start of Spring, it was warmer than average.
Both Wellington and New Plymouth were 14 degrees overnight.
Some areas quickly got warmer on Friday, like Napier rising from 7 degrees to 17 degrees within about an hour.
The strong wind dragging warm air will make its way across the country today, finishing in Auckland and Northland this evening.
"These fronts are continuing their march across the country, weakening as they do so."
Heavy rain warnings were also in place for the headwaters of the Canterbury Lakes and rivers until 8am on Friday, and the Tararua Range until 1pm.
A road snowfall warning is also in place for Milford Rd (SH94) until 6pm on Friday, with the possibility of 2cm to 5cm of snow accumulating by the tunnel.
The weekend was looking more settled, according to MetService, with some rain. The North Island would see a few showers in the west on Saturday, but be mainly fine while the South Island could expect rain or showers in the west and south with possible heavy falls.
On Sunday, MetService said rain would be developing in the west with possible heavy falls for the North Island and rain the west and south with heavy falls for the South Island.
Wind threatens Auckland Harbour Bridge closure
Travel across the Auckland Harbour Bridge might be disrupted on Friday, transport officials have warned.
Gusts of up to 80km/h have been forecast between midday and 4pm.
"Motorists are advised to drive to the conditions and pay attention to electronic message boards on the motorway, which will advise if any lane closures and reduced speed limits are required," the New Zealand Transport Agency said in a statement on Thursday.
"If there is potential for sudden and high wind gusts on the bridge, lowering the speed limit gives motorists time to react and take more care."

title: Power cuts remain for some in North Island after stormy weather
text:
Power cuts remain for some in North Island after stormy weather
Weather warnings are no longer in place, but Monday's strong winds in the Hawke's Bay left hundreds without electricity.
Powerco's website showed 136 power cuts across the Manawatū-Whanganui, Taranaki, Bay of Plenty, and Waikato regions.
Powerco said 44 properties in Ashhurst had been without power since 7.05pm on Monday due to a fault on the feeder.
The electricity company said a power cut affecting 13 properties in Ashhurst since Monday afternoon appeared to be wind-related, but was still under investigation.
It said a smaller power cut in Upokongaro, affecting six properties, was due to trees hitting lines on Monday afternoon.
Powerco crews were assessing affected sites and working to restore power, it said.
Unison's website showed about 40 properties without electricity in Hastings, Napier, and Taupō.

images.caption: A map on Powerco's website showing outages on Tuesday 1 September 2026. Somne were due to high winds on Monday. Photo credit: Powerco

title: Nepal floods: Save the Children reunites 69 children with their families
text:
International aid organisation Save the Children has been able to reunite 69 children with their families in Nepal in the aftermath of flash flooding on Wednesday.
At least 682 people have died and close to 3000 are missing after a wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing entire villages.
Five New Zealanders are believed to be missing. They have been named by friends and family as Mihir Patel, Kinnari Patel, Shweta Mhatre, Dejan Kuzmic and Suhasini Reddy.
Save the Children's Amy Sawitta Lefevre told RNZ that it was still a search and rescue operation, with her organisation distributing water and food, providing temporary shelter, and administering medical care.
Sawitta Lefevre has been in Nuwakot, 50 to 75 kilometres northwest of Kathmandu, since Friday.
"We have - and the number may have gone up since - but over the past 24 hours, 48 hours or so, we have managed to reunite about 69 children with their families. And that's been wonderful to see.
"But obviously there's many, many more out there who will need to be reunited with their families as well."
One of the most urgent concerns for Save the Children was family separation, she said, with children as young as five seeking help.
Some children were still wearing the clothes they were wearing when the disaster hit, she told RNZ.
"We saw lots of kids with grey and muddy clothes, and the children were obviously, you know, they were in need of water, they were in need of food, they were in need of blankets, and they're also in need of medical assistance."
Some children had developed upper respiratory tract infections from being exposed to the elements for so long.
Overcrowded temporary shelters were another concern. Sawitta Lefevre said the number of children at one holding centre had doubled from 30 to 60 within a couple of hours.
The overcrowding risked spreading disease, as well as affecting children's mental health and meaning less protection for them.
Save the Children expected to remain in Nepal for some time to provide humanitarian assistance.
"We are looking to stay in Nepal on this response, on this flood response, for a very long time. I mean, we're talking months, if not a year or more here.
"The humanitarian needs are many and it's not something that we're going to be able to deal with overnight or in a matter of days or weeks. So we're definitely in this for the long haul," Sawitta Lefevre said.

title: Heavy rain for upper North Island, avalanche risk ongoing for South Island
text:
Heavy rain for upper North Island, avalanche risk ongoing for South Island
A flood alert has been issued for Warkworth and forecasters have upgraded weather warnings for the upper North Island, as heavy rain is expected to sweep down from the north through into early Sunday, while strong wind watches and avalanche warnings are in place for parts of the South Island.
On Saturday, MetService upgraded earlier weather watches to orange Heavy Rain Warnings, for Northland, Auckland, Coromandel Peninsula, Bay of Plenty, and some parts of Tai Rāwhiti.
Up to 100mm could fall at rates up to 40mm an hour, though localised downpours could mean even higher amounts. The warnings were expected to be in place until 2am Sunday for Auckland, 3am for Coromandel, and 5am for Bay of Plenty and Tai Rāwhiti.
MetService warned people in all orange heavy rain warning areas to clear their drains and gutters, avoid low-lying areas and drive carefully. Waterways could rise rapidly.
A yellow heavy rain watch was also in place for Waikato.
Flood warning for Warkworth river, Aucklanders warned localised rain could be intense
Auckland Emergency Management (AEM) said a flood alert had been issued for Falls Road in Warkworth, on the Mahurangi River: "Please avoid taking Falls Road, particularly the sections where the road fords the river or that are typically affected by flooding".
People in the Falls Road area of Warkworth should delay travel if they could, it said: "Stay safe - never drive through floodwaters".
The Mahurangi River was already swollen by late Saturday afternoon, Auckland Emergency Management general manager Adam Maggs said, and there had been steady rain throughout the day.
Auckland's Hisbiscus Coast Highway was closed between Hatfields Beach and Waiwera on Saturday night.
AEM said a slip had been reported, and an assessment was being carried out. A spokesperson says there were no signs of property damage, and traffic management was in place.
The forecast heavy rain in localised patches could mean flooding, Maggs said, and AEM teams would be keeping a close eye on the wider north and northwest parts of Auckland.
"It is very hard to determine where that is going to be. (MetService) are not expecting problems to be broad-scale across the whole region, so we have our contractors focusing on the areas that are typically the hot spots, and we have it well covered."
There had only been a few call outs by late Saturday, which was typical of a rainy wintry day, Maggs said.
In Auckland, any blocked stormwater drainage should be reported to Auckland Council on 09 301 0101.
Avalanche risk and strong wind watches for South Island areas, continued storm mop up in Queenstown
In the South Island, yellow strong wind watches were issued for parts of Southland and Otago, along with some road snowfall warnings, while Queenstown continues its clean up efforts after it was hit by wild weather this week, causing flooding, slips and road closures.
On Thursday night, 45 people were evacuated from their homes across the Queenstown Lakes District during the storm. And firefighters went to about 16 flooding-related jobs, in Queenstown, Frankton, Arrrowtown, Wānaka and Lake Hāwea.
Queenstown Mayor John Glover said he hopes residents will be able to return to their homes as soon as possible. He did not know how many people were still unable to return, but was expecting assessments would continue throughout the weekend.
The Civil Defence Welfare Hub at the Queenstown Memorial Centre was still open, Glover said.
On Saturday, the New Zealand Avalanche Advisory (which is run by the Mountain Safety Council) warned there was a high avalanche danger in mountainous areas throughout most of the South Island.
Warnings were issued for many areas, including Aoraki Mt Cook, Arthur's Pass, Ohau, Queenstown, Wānaka, and Aspiring, with some noting varied risks for different places within those areas.
Aoraki Mt Cook, and parts of Queenstown were noted in particular.
Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley said it had received reports of significant avalanches coming down to the valley floor: "This is not just a warning to alpine skiers and people heading into high alpine regions and backcountry.
"If people are considering going tramping into sub alpine regions you need to be aware of the hazards above you."
People should check the avalanche forecast before heading into alpine backcountry, Daisley said.
In the North Island, Tongariro and Taranaki were also under considerable risk of avalanches as well.
Traffic congestion after road closures and slips
A number of road closures have also impacted the Queenstown region, which caused significant congestion in the town on Friday.
Fernhill and Sunshine Bay Community Association's Simone Bray said restrictions at the one mile roundabout brought commuters to a standstill.
"We live on the top of a really big hill so there's no active transport option for us either so we were sort of just advised if you don't have to go anywhere just stay at home.
"The traffic was built up but it was taking people about an hour and a half basically just to go down the hill to get into Queenstown, which is normally a four minute drive."
Residents in Fernhill, Sunshine Bay, Queenstown central and Frankton Road were also asked to conserve water.
There had been more than 20 slips, many of them substantial on the stretch between Lake Hāwea and Makarora.
Two cars and their occupants were freed after being trapped between slips on State Highway 6 near Wānaka on Friday.
The section of SH6 would remain closed all weekend, NZTA said.

images.caption: Heavy rain is expected on Saturday into early Sunday for much of the upper North Island. Photo credit: Supplied/ MetService
Heavy flooding on Thursday, in Queenstown. RNZ / Katie Todd
The Avalanche Advisory said the risk was especially high for Aoraki Mt Cook. Unsplash / Corey Serravite
Roads were impacted in Queenstown's CBD after the storm on Thursday. RNZ / Katie Todd

title: Wet weekend in store for Northland, Auckland; worst over for South Island
text:
Winter storm hits the South Island
People were evacuated in Queenstown overnight as a significant winter storm battered the South Island.
Firefighters went to about 16 flooding-related jobs during Thursday night across Queenstown, Frankton, Arrrowtown, Wanaka and Lake Hāwea.
In some cases, water went into homes.
Fire and Emergency says a number of properties were evacuated around Fernhill because of concerns about slips and land instability.
It says there were many other calls about flooded roads and sections that firefighters didn't attend.
The South Island has been hit with a massive winter storm which has brought heavy rain, flooding, rockfall, slips and snow.
More than 300 millimetres of rain has fallen in Franz Josef while more than 20 centimetres of snow fell in some parts of the South Island on Thursday.
Queenstown Lakes District Council says its emergency operations centre has been busy overnight responding to issues caused by heavy rain.
It has set up a civil defence welfare hub in Queenstown overnight to support people.
In a social media post, it says multiple slips, washouts, rockfalls, and surface flooding are affecting the roading network, particularly on Haast Pass Road, Luggate Hill, Tarras Road, and Kingston Road. "Expect delays, traffic management, and ongoing disruptions throughout the day," the post says.
The council is asking people to avoid unnecessary travel and take extra care on the roads.
Surface flooding, debris, and other hazards may still pose some risks.
Highway closures
State Highway 6 between Makarora and Lake Hāwea has been closed due to a slip on Friday morning.
Motorists were urged to avoid the area or delay their trip.
The Transport Agency said slips, rockfalls and treefalls were a continuing concern.
State Highway 94 to Milford Sound remains closed from the Lower Hollyford Road intersection to Donne River due to the avalanche risk.
It is not expected to reopen until Saturday.
The Crown Range Road was closed on Friday morning between Eastburn Road and Cardrona.
The Transport Agency has area warnings for surface flooding for State Highway 6 from Haast to Hokitika, State Highway 8A from Tarras to Luggate, State Highway 8 from Omarama to Clearburn, and for snow from Springfield to Otira on State Highway 73.
Fresh heavy rain watches
MetService has issued new heavy rain watches for Northland, Auckland, Great Barrier Island, Coromandel Peninsula and Bay of Plenty.
Northland's watch will run from 4am to 10pm on Saturday, while for Auckland, Great Barrier Island, Coromandel Peninsula it will apply from 9am to midnight on Saturday.
Bay of Plenty about and west of the Rangitaiki River may see periods of heavy rain from noon to midnight, MetService says, with the watch also affecting areas east of the river from 3pm on Saturday to 3am on Sunday.
Orange heavy rain warnings cover Westland and headwaters of lakes and rivers in Otago and Canterbury with a separate warning starting from midnight for the Grey and Buller ranges.
An area warning for surface flooding remained overnight for State Highway 6 from Haast to Hokitika.
The Transport Agency says all highways except part of State Highway 94 to Milford Sound are open.
Strong wind watches are also in place for Wairarapa south of Masterton, Wellington and the Marlborough Sounds from 6am to 8pm on Friday. Northwest winds may approach severe gale in exposed places, MetService says.
A strong wind watch was also in place until 8am for the Canterbury High Country north of Mt Cook.
Worst over for South Island
MetService's head of weather Heather Keats told Morning Report the snow had more or less finished while the rain band was tracking north.
The "decent totals" of rainfall in the last 12 hours included 90-130mm for the Westland Ranges and the Canterbury headwaters while 90mm had fallen in Whataroa nearer to the coast.
"So those river networks are really high, they're going to take quite a few days to clear out but the heavy rain warnings will all have expired by midday."
The wind watches would be affecting "the usual suspects" and had included gusts of 230km/h for the Canterbury high country overnight.
"So a bit breezy for your Friday."
The northerly feed was hitting the Alps and becomes a norwester which would see Christchurch hit a high of 20 degrees Celsius today, she said.
However, a new low will move over Northland, Auckland and the Coromandel heading on to Gisborne and bringing heavy rain for those areas over the weekend.
"The weather has decided the meteorological spring has started - we're going to see those relentless westerlies, fast-moving features and this weekend is going to be one of those weekends."
Keats expected heavy rain watches to be issued on Saturday but the positive was that any bad weather would be fast-moving.
She said Christchurch would be "the pick of the bunch" over the weekend while Auckland would be "a bit of a write-off".
High avalanche risk
South Island ski fields on high alert for avalanches
The Mountain Safety Council has warned of high avalanche danger across the Southern Alps.
The council says naturally triggered avalanches are likely and human-triggered avalanches are very likely across the Arthur's Pass, Aoraki /Mt Cook, Ohau, Queenstown, Wanaka, and Aspiring regions.
NZ Ski chief executive Paul Anderson said Mt Hutt was closed this morning, Coronet Peak was open, and the road to the Remarkables was still being assessed before a decision was made on opening the skifield.
He said the avalanche conditions were unusual at present because the snowfall had been followed by rain saturating the snow and making it heavier and increasing the avalanche risk.
Patrol teams were monitoring the conditions 24/7 to ensure the skifields were safe, he said.
He did not expect explosives would need to be used to move some of the snow, instead, skicutting (skiing across a diagonal angle across the slope to assess its stability) and trails would have been groomed overnight.
"Our focus will be on the known avalanche zones within our ski area boundaries."
He said if the skifields were open customers could be confident they were safe.

title: West Coast in for a lashing of heavy rain over next three days
text:
Weather warnings for parts of South Island
Canterbury's rivers are on the rise as heavy rain hits the South Island - but they are not expected break their banks.
Canterbury Regional Council says rain is falling on the alpine headwater of the Rangitata, Rakaia, Waimakariri, Hurunui and Waiau-uha rivers, but it is expected to turn to snow later this afternoon.
The council said the river flows will increase in the upper parts of these rivers this afternoon and are expected to boost flows in the lower areas from this evening.
The council urged anyone who is working or recreating in these riverbeds to be prepared for increasing flows, but said out-of-river flooding was unlikely from any of these rivers.
River flows are expected to remain high on Friday.
Driving conditions
NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi said snow and heavy rain were making driving treacherous on state highways about the South Island.
The agency said surface flooding was affecting State Highway 1 - south of Dunedin - while an area warning was place on SH6 between Makarora and Fox Glacier - as heavy rains forecast for the next three days arrived on western parts of the island.
Meanwhile, a section of SH94 - between Te Anau and Milford Sound - was likely to remain closed until Friday due to avalanche risk.
MetService had a Heavy Snow Watch in place for the Canterbury high country - south of the Rangitata River, and Otago - north of Arrowtown to Ranfurly.
Up to 20cm of snow was predicted for SH73 through the Arthur's Pass, while up to 15cm of snow was forecast to fall over the Lindis Pass summit on SH8.
Overnight snowfalls were also expected on SH8 and SH80 - north of Twizel.
Motorists were advised to expect further closures and people travelling in affected areas should reduce speeds and be prepared for delays with warm clothing, food and water.
A deluge and heavy snow is expected to lash parts of the South Island as a complex low pressure system hits.
MetService has upgraded a heavy rain watch to an orange warning for Grey and Buller south of Westport.
Up to 90 millimetres of rain is expected to fall, particularly around the Paparoa Range, from 6pm on Wednesday over 12 hours.
An orange heavy rain for Westland was in place between Wednesday morning and Friday afternoon with up to 450mm expected to fall about the ranges and up to 200mm closer to the coast.
MetService warned that surface flooding, slips and difficult driving conditions were possible and streams and rivers might rise rapidly.
The rain was expected to fall as heavy snow about inland parts of the Canterbury High Country and inland Otago between Arrowtown to Ranfurly and might approaching warning levels above 800 metres overnight on Wednesday until 6pm on Thursday.
MetService said lesser amounts of snow could fall as low as 400m and it had a moderate change of becoming a warning.
MetService meteorologist Braydon White said farmers on the eastern side of the divide of the central South Island - including Mount Cook and potentially Twizel - should prepare livestock for a sudden shift from previously warm conditions to a significant amount of snow.
"Going into a much colder situation in the next couple of days, you'll want to make sure that your livestock are doing okay, making sure you have plans in place if you've got any young lambs starting to appear," White said.
He said motorists in the area should consider changing their routes to avoid the higher passes and ensure they had snow chains, sleeping bags, warm clothing, and emergency items with them.
"If you do have to travel, maybe consider having a go bag in your car, just in case you get trapped," White said.
Meanwhile, on the western side of the island, a low pressure system - which was travelling down from the east coast of Australia - could see up to 450mm of rain about the Westland ranges with nearly 200mm expected to fall nearer the coast.
The rain was expected to peak at three points across the coming days - reaching up to 30 mm/h on Wednesday afternoon and evening, then again on Thursday evening and in a final burst on Friday morning.
"This fairly complex system is quite wavy and so what happens is you get one wave pushing into the Alps, dumping a whole lot of rain and then it'll ease off for a bit of time as the next wave approaches from the sea.
"So part of the reason this is such an extended period is because we're capturing two or three waves as they all funnel through," White said.
White said the drawn-out nature of the rainfall could make the rain across the area a little less severe than the numbers might initially suggest.
"Because it's not all falling in a very short amount of time, that gives time for the rivers to really just get the water away. So while it is quite a bit of rain, if there was anywhere in the country that was going to handle that reasonably well, it would be Westland.
"Certainly there's risk of rivers rising rapidly or slips and potentially road disruption for a time of flooding that could cut places off. But it's hard to be more certain about just how bad it could get," White said.
A heavy rain warning is also in place for Grey and Buller south of Westport.
"So while we're expecting the focus of that rain to be the Westland area, the waviness of the system does mean that it moves north and south at times, and so certainly outside of that Westland area we'll still see some decent bursts of heavy rain.
"Alongside that, the north-westerly system will be a bit stronger and that will allow that rain to push over the Alps and into the Canterbury and Otago headwaters as well," White said.
MetService said there was a high chance of the rain watches being upgraded to warnings.

title: Heavy rain and snow on way for South Island
text:
Heavy rain and snow on way for South Island
MetService is warning of significant rain and snow for parts of the South Island, with an Orange heavy rain warning issued for Westland.
A slow moving front will bring a prolonged period of heavy rain from midday Wednesday which could become heavy snow in parts of inland Otago and South Canterbury.
In Westland 400 to 500 millimetres of rain could fall in the ranges, and between 150 and 200 millimetres closer to the coast, with heavy bursts from Wednesday afternoon.
MetService said there was a low chance of an upgrade to a red warning.
People in the area are advised to clear their drains and gutters, and to avoid low-lying areas, and warned that streams and rivers could rise rapidly and there could be surface flooding and slips.
There is also a heavy rain watch for Grey District, Fiordland and the headwaters of Canterbury and Otago lakes and rivers from tomorrow morning.
The Canterbury High Country, south of Rangitata River, and in Otago, north of Arrowtown to Ranfurly, could be in for heavy snow.
From 6pm on Wednesday, MetService is forecasting heavy snow above 800 metres, and lesser amounts down to 400 metres.
In the higher areas snowfall may approach warning criteria.
MetService said the snow could cause damage to trees and powerlines, stress livestock and disrupt travel.
People in those areas are advised to prepare for cold temperatures and snow, and for possible power outages.
If people must travel MetService said they should ensure they have snow chains, sleeping bags, warm clothing, and emergency items.

images.caption: Photo credit: RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

title: South Island braces for winter storm with snow and heavy rain on the way
text:
A significant winter storm will hit the South Island as the week progresses, MetService says.
The forecaster said while warm northwesterly winds would bring notably warmer temperatures to the North Island from Wednesday, heavy rain would be developing in the South Island.
A prolonged period of wet weather was expected, it said, particularly in the west of the South Island.
A cooler southerly air would follow late Wednesday and Thursday with warning amounts of snow possible to 400m for inland parts of South Canterbury and Otago.
"The weather becomes increasingly active across the South Island from Wednesday as a slow-moving low in the Tasman Sea directs a large amount of moisture toward the island. Significant severe weather is expected with this event," MetService warned.
MetService meteorologist Devlin Lynden said rain would become widespread and heavy on Wednesday with the worst hitting the Southern Alps and West Coast, where a heavy rain watch was in place.
Further warnings were likely, Lynden said, and heavy falls were possible across much of the South Island.
The low was expected to be slow moving, he said, and could bring prolonged heavy rainfall for Central Otago, the Queenstown Lakes District, the Mackenzie Basin and inland Canterbury.
Anyone planning travel or outdoor activities in the South Island later this week, particularly in western and central areas was encouraged to keep up to date with the latest forecasts and warnings or watches on the MetService website.
Lynden said the North Island would remain comparatively settled throughout the first half of the week, with light winds and dry weather.
Throughout the week, northwesterlies would push a warmer airmass across the island, with temperatures becoming notably warmer. Lynden said most places should remain dry.

images.caption: Rain in the South Island would become widespread and heavy on Wednesday. (File photo) Photo credit: RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

title: Weather: Heavy rain warnings for South Island, severe gales to batter lower North Island
text:
Weather: Heavy rain warnings for South Island, severe gales to batter lower North Island
Heavy rain is expected to hit southern regions over the weekend.
MetService said western areas of the South Island were likely to get heavy rain on Saturday.
Severe gales would follow on Sunday, while snow would fall in Otago and high-altitude roads across the South Island.
"A series of fronts, embedded within a strong and moist northwest flow, move over New Zealand today and tomorrow, followed by a change to strong, colder southwesterlies," the forecaster said on Saturday morning, urging people to keep up to date.
A heavy rain watch was issued for Westland and areas south of Aoraki/Mt Cook, lasting from 9am Saturday to 9am Sunday. Thunderstorms were possible, with a moderate chance of upgrading to a warning.
Orange strong wind warnings were also in place for Tararua District, Wairarapa, Wellington and Marlborough Sounds for Sunday morning.
A heavy snow watch will be in place for Southern Lakes and Central Otago from 5am to 4pm Sunday, above 700m, with a moderate chance of upgrading to a warning.
And MetService said strong wind was possible for inland Hawke's Bay about and south of State Highway 5 between 8am and 2pm Sunday; and in Marlborough about and east of the Kaikoura ranges between 7am and 3pm Sunday.
Both areas could experience severe gales in exposed places.

images.caption: A woman has difficulty holding an umbrella from strong winds in rainy weather. Photo credit: 123RF

title: South and lower North Island in for a weekend of strong winds and rain
text:
For many parts of the country, instructions for the weekend include tying down trampolines and keeping campervans home in preparation for strong winds and rain.
MetService has issued several wind and rain warnings for both the North and South Islands.
Meteorologist Alwyn Bakker said there was a series of fronts moving over the South Island from the southwest and bringing with it heavy rain and wind strength changes.
"Behind that front, kind of on the Sunday, we're getting strong, cold southwesterlies coming through.
"So what we're expecting wind wise, they're going to be very strong."
An orange strong wind warning is in place from very early on Sunday till the afternoon for Tararua District, Wairarapa, Canterbury High Country, Wellington and the Marlborough Sounds and Southland - south of Gore, including Stewart Island.
Dunedin and Clutha were under a yellow strong wind watch.
Bakker said in exposed areas there was a risk of severe westerly gales reaching 120 kilometres an hour - particularly for Southland.
"If you've got any items that can be picked up by strong winds, you should be preparing.
"Tie your trampolines down, that kind of stuff, and there's a risk of damage to trees and power lines and driving might be difficult, especially for campervans."
Bakker said heavy rain was less widespread than strong wind this weekend but still important.
An orange heavy rain warning was in place for the ranges of Buller and Grey Districts from 3pm Saturday till 9am Sunday.
Bakker said 90 to 120 millimetres of rain was expected over that time and thunderstorms were possible on Sunday morning. There was a minimal chance of upgrading to a red warning.
Yellow heavy rain watches were also issued for the headwaters of the Canterbury lakes and rivers and ranges of Westland District. The rain watches had a moderate chance of upgrading to a rain warning.
"Streams and rivers might rise rapidly, there might be surface flooding, there might be slips," Bakker said.
"We recommend before all of that comes through, just check your drains and gutters to make sure they're all clear."
While there are no snow warnings of any type, some snow was possible for higher roads in the South Island.
Bakker said the strong cold south westerlies expected would drag cooler air from the Southern Ocean. However, it was still unclear how well that would line up with the rain.
"Because there's no good whatsoever if you have lots of warm rain and then the cold air comes through afterwards. You won't get snow."
Bakker recommended that people check back again on Saturday for the latest warnings.
As for the upper North Island, it is currently free from any warnings and watches but that doesn't mean clear weather is expected.
"There's going to be a bit of rain for the upper North Island. It doesn't look anywhere near as heavy as it would be for Westland. Winds don't look too strong through there."
While the weekend is not looking good for most of the country, the beginning of next week is looking somewhat brighter.
"It's going to be another absolutely classic, the weekend is horrible and then it kind of goes all right for the work week.
"We're going to be getting a bit of a ridge building... so we've got a pretty minimal risk of anything happening Monday, Tuesday when it comes to severe weather."

images.caption: A series of fronts moving over the country are responsible for the weekends poor weather. Photo credit: MetService/Screenshot

title: More than 180,000 without power in Hawaii, 100 homes damaged as Lala weakens to tropical storm
text:
More than 180,000 without power in Hawaii, 100 homes damaged as Lala weakens to tropical storm
More than 180,000 utility customers remained without power across Hawaii on Sunday afternoon after Hurricane Lala brushed the Big Island before being downgraded to a tropical storm.
Some 183,123 customers across Hawaii were without power as of 3:30pm local time, according to poweroutage.us.
Outages in Oahu, the most populated island, had dropped from more than 220,000 to about 130,000 as of Sunday morning, state officials said during a press conference.
State officials received reports of at least 100 homes damaged, Hawaii Governor Josh Green said on Sunday.
At 2pm, Lala was moving west towards southwest Kauai County at about 31km/h, with maximum sustained winds near 105km/h, just below the hurricane threshold of 119km/h, according to the latest advisory from the National Hurricane Center.
A tropical storm warning remained in effect for Kauai county, although those warnings for Maui and Oahu counties were discontinued earlier on Sunday, according to the hurricane centre. The weather agency's projections indicated that if the storm remained on its expected path, it should be clear of Hawaii's islands by 8am local time.
Hawaiian Electric had warned customers on Saturday evening that repair efforts were being hampered as hurricane-force winds toppled trees and rain flooded roadways.
Lala had battered parts of Hawaii with flash floods "like we've never seen", a state official said.
State officials also urged residents to stay indoors after at least one person was reported dead in a car-related accident.
"It's not a day to go to the beach," one official said during a press conference on Sunday morning.
Video released by the Hawaii Department of Transportation showed floodwaters overtaking roads. Two homes were swept away, according to the National Weather Service.
About 117 people were in shelters as of Sunday morning, officials said.
The Hawaii Department of Transportation said all airports had reopened, but state officials advised travellers to check with their airlines for updates.
- Reuters

images.caption: A police officer monitors traffic after metal and wooden debris fell from the roof of the Sheraton Princess Kaiulani hotel in the Waikiki neighbourhood in Honolulu during the storm. Photo credit: AFP / Eugene Tanner

title: Wintry blast to bring snow, frost and rain
text:
Wintry blast to bring snow, frost and rain
Temperatures in some areas will get as cold as -9 overnight, says MetService.
The Twizel and Mount Cook area will be almost double digits in the negative.

All state highways in the South Island are open this morning, despite snow sweeping through overnight.
However the Transport Agency says motorists should take care on the roads where snow has settled.

title: Japan's record rains strand thousands at Narita airport
text:
Japan's record rains strand thousands at Narita airport
Record rainfall in Japan stranded thousands of travellers at Tokyo's Narita airport on Friday, bringing floods to the surrounding area that disrupted transport, knocked out power to 20,000 homes and killed eight.
During one of Japan's busiest holiday weeks, more than 360mm of rain fell in 24 hours in parts of the Chiba area adjoining Tokyo, inundating roads and railways, with soldiers sent to help with rescue efforts.
"This case was an extremely unusual situation," Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters. "I have responded to many disasters in the past, but I have never experienced a case like this."
The eight dead included one person trapped in a submerged vehicle, public broadcaster NHK said, citing Chiba authorities and police.
At Narita, airport staff distributed sleeping bags, water and snacks to hundreds of passengers, many of whom had bedded down on Thursday after transport disruptions stranded about 7,000 people, causing widespread chaos.
"I queued for a taxi, but the wait was four hours," said Minoru Yamasaki, a 48-year-old Chiba resident returning from holiday, who had booked a hotel only to be told it could not put him up. With nowhere else to go, he returned to the airport.
Japan Airlines said some flights may experience delays but no cancellations were currently expected. Some major highways in Chiba were shut, forcing drivers onto alternative routes and causing heavy traffic, according to highway operator NEXCO East.
An airport spokesperson said most flights were expected to operate normally on Friday.
More than 20,000 homes were without power in the early hours of Friday, after rain flooded a power substation, utility Tokyo Electric Power said, while gas supply to nearly 13,000 was temporarily cut.
In Chiba city, one of the worst-hit spots, hundreds of people spent the night under foil blankets at makeshift evacuation centres in government buildings.
Some major highways in Chiba were shut, forcing drivers to take alternative routes that clogged traffic, said highway operator NEXCO East.
Several rail services were also suspended on Friday, though some services from Narita to Tokyo resumed, easing congestion at the international transport hub.
Weather authorities said the 367mm of rain over a 24-hour period in Chiba exceeded the previous record of 309mm set in October 2013.
- Reuters

images.caption: An aerial photo shows widespread flooding around JR Oami Station following torrential rain in Oamishirasato City, Chiba Prefecture, Japan, on August 14, 2026. Photo credit: DAISUKE URAKAMI
Cars pass a commuter on a flooded road near Chiba metro station in Chiba. PHILIP FONG

title: Gisborne residents urged to be ready for flooding and slips
text:
MetService says about 40 millimetres of rain has already fallen in Gisborne, after a heavy downpour and thunderstorms on Friday morning.
The weather agency says the area west of Hicks Bay on the East Cape has been worst hit.
It said it was monitoring the Poroporo River which had accumulated 55mm in the last 12 hours.
A line of thunderstorms around the Oweka Bridge had weakened and ceased since midday, it said.
Gisborne's Civil Defence said it had not seen any critical risk and had heard of one incident of minor surface flooding.
Tairāwhiti Civil Defence is urging residents to be ready for potential surface flooding, slips and more as heavy rain moves in.
An orange heavy rain warning is in effect for Gisborne/Tai Rāwhiti, north of Tolaga Bay, until 8pm on Friday night.
"That's in place this morning and 25 millimetres per hour rain rate can cause that rapid flooding. Some places are already seeing quite high rain rate," meteorologist Paris Mitchell said.
Between 90 and 120mm of rain is expected.
The public are being told to clear gutters and drains, steer clear of low-lying areas while the heaviest rain comes through, and drive to the conditions.
MetService said there was only a minimal chance of upgrading its warning to red.
The worst of the weather is forecast for the morning and afternoon - with a thunderstorm warning in place for then.
Gisborne mayor Rehette Stolz asked the public to report any flooding or slips amid heavy downpours.
She said it was very wet but Gisborne was prepared for anything, and civil defence teams were monitoring water levels and flooding.
She reminded people to be cautious and drive to conditions.
MetService said it has recorded up to 10mm of rain per hour already this morning in the northern ranges and 8mm around East Cape.
Earlier, MetService issued a severe thunderstorm warning for the Far North.
The thunderstorms were expected to come with torrential rain.

title: Downpours on the radar for East Coast, Bay of Plenty regions
text:
Downpours on the radar for East Coast, Bay of Plenty regions
Tairāwhiti Civil Defence is warning residents to brace for torrential rain forecast to hit from Thursday night.
MetService has issued a heavy rain warning for Gisborne-Tai Rāwhiti north of Tolaga Bay for 22 hours from 10pm tonight until 8pm on Friday.
It says to expect from 90mm to 120mm of rain.
Tairāwhiti Civil Defence is urging people to clear gutters and drains immediately and avoid low-lying areas.
"You know the drill folks, streams and rivers may rise rapidly. Surface flooding, slips, and difficult driving conditions possible."
A heavy rain warning is currently in place for Bay of Plenty west of Kawerau until 3pm on Thursday.
MetService says Tauranga is having its wettest day of the month so far.
Areas in Bay of Plenty have already seen significant amounts of rain, with some MetService stations reporting over 50 millimetres of rain in the 12 hours up to 11am.
A low pressure centre from the Tasman sea is driving persistant rain over the northeastern of parts of the North Island.
The wet weather is expected to continue through to Sunday.
The weather forecaster says localised downpours of more than 25mm are possible during the warning period.
Up to 80mm of rain might fall on top of what has already been experienced.
While the warning expires mid-afternoon, the rain may continue until early Friday morning, MetService says.
A heavy rain watch is also in place for Bay of Plenty east of Kawerau for 19 hours from 2pm today through until 9am on Friday.
There might be some heavy rain during this time, it says.
The wet weather is expected to continue through to Sunday.

title: Yellow rain watches issued for Northland, Auckland and Westland
text:
Yellow rain watches issued for Northland, Auckland and Westland
Northern and eastern areas of Northland and Auckland north of Orewa are under a heavy rain watch on Wednesday.
The watches which also cover Great Barrier Island came into effect at 10am, MetService says.
A low-pressure system southwest of New Zealand is driving a frontal band of rain eastwards, mainly affecting the top half of the North Island and Westland today.
The forecast which applies for the upper North Island through to 1am on Thursday is for periods of rain with some heavy falls, and the amounts may approach the criteria for an upgrade to a warning.
The rainfall could be 25-40 mm/h with or without lightning and a low risk of thunderstorms.
The rain will ease from the north on Wednesday afternoon and evening, MetService says.
"The air-mass associated with the front is very warm and moist, especially for late winter," it says.
Meanwhile, in the South Island, there will be periods of heavy rain from 2pm today through until 6am tomorrow in Westland.
The rainfall may be especially heavy about the ranges.
The band of rain has made its way to Aotearoa from the Tasman Sea and might result in rain and showers for most of the North Island on Thursday.
MetService said temperatures were looking almost balmy compared to last week's polar blast, with overnight lows in the single digits rather than the negatives and afternoons climbing into the mid-teens across the North Island.

title: 'No one wanted to make that decision' - road closure calls go unheard during violent storm
text:
'No one wanted to make that decision' - road closure calls go unheard during violent storm
A South Westland farmer and councillor on the West Coast Regional Council wants to see better communication during storms, saying crucial communication with the New Zealand Transport Agency remains elusive.
Councillor Andy Campbell told the council's Operations Committee meeting last week that a lineman for Westpower had wanted to close State Highway 6 through to Whataroa during a fierce windstorm on 6 July, but was unable to do so.
Gale-force winds had already knocked down power-lines around Te Taho, near the Whataroa River gorge, and the local fire brigade reported that its fire-fighters were getting blown over by the strength of the wind.
It was also the same day Associate Minister for Regional Development Mark Patterson was due to open the upgraded stopbanks on the south side of the Waiho (Waiau) River. The official function was cancelled due to the storm.
Campbell said the lineman could not contact anyone in authority to request the road closed.
"They had trouble getting hold of anybody to close the road. At 4 or 5 in the afternoon, there were campervans getting blown off the road ... Just could not get anybody to close the road."
Other places on the West Coast were unaware of emergencies that took place in the more remote areas of the region.
"We need to be able to communicate a bit better and that just proves that one small area of the West Coast is having an emergency and a lot of other places are unaware of it."
Hari Hari Fire and Emergency NZ volunteer Shirley Black told Local Democracy Reporting she had called NZTA's transport operations in Wellington but they had been unable to help.
"I did speak to them at one stage. They were full of sympathy but do nothing, which is not helpful when you are in that situation. It is hard to imagine what it is like when you are not here. You try to explain an emergency situation and somebody hundreds of miles away has no idea what you are talking about."
She said the windstorm had begun early in the morning and was too strong for people to be on the road.
"Being with FENZ, we were being called out to vehicles that were being blown over, and it just seemed to me that it was a situation where the road should be closed and people should be staying where they were."
Black said she tried calling different agencies from two in the afternoon to get the road closed but did not hear back from them.
"I tried from about 2 o'clock in the afternoon to get that to happen. It seemed to me that no one wanted to make that decision."
The highway was finally closed at 6pm that day after she spoke to other local FENZ brigades on the West Coast.
"The commander here on the Coast got on to it and I think he spoke to Civil Defence, the roading people and was able to make them aware of how serious the situation was," Black said.
Responding today, an NZTA spokesman said State Highway 6 had been closed in the morning for three hours due to winds, but NZTA was requested to close the road later in the day due to risks to road users. Although a decision to close State Highway 6 was considered, it decided not to close the road because the situation could be handled better if it remained open.
"NZTA, in discussion with its team/contractor on the ground on the West Coast, considered this, but the decision made at that time was not to close the road. This was based on NZTA's responsibilities and the view from the team/contractor that the situation could be best managed by keeping the road open.
"While the wind posed a risk, it was only specific types of vehicles most exposed to this risk, such as higher-sided vehicles. NZTA's decision was conveyed at the time to the emergency services," the spokesman said.
NZTA made its decisions on highway closures based on the travelling public and the best information available at the time.
"Ultimately, NZTA makes its decisions about the need for any highway closures or restrictions based on its responsibilities to the travelling public and the best information available to it, including the advice of those on the ground."
WCRC office of the chief executive group manager Jo Field said although the regional council was involved with responding to the emergency on July 6, responsibility lies with NZTA.
Councillor Chris Coll asked whether the mayor of Westland could have declared a local emergency.
Field said that was possible.
"You can even declare for small areas, if you need to."
Coll noted that one of the criteria for declaring an emergency was if local services cannot cope with a weather event.
Field said local services would need to inform Emergency Management (Civil Defence) of that scenario.
"You need the local services to actually inform Emergency Management that they are not coping for that to happen, so it comes down to the communication with groups such as NZTA."
Campbell said the chief fire officer at Hari Hari had also tried to get the State Highway closed but "did not have any luck".
"They need to be able to get a hold of NZTA or whomever to get the traffic control out there."
Coll said the local fire stations could instead contact the regional council, which could then declare an emergency through the mayor.
"They contact council, and council, through the mayor, can declare if the threshold is reached."
However, Campbell was adamant that local services needed to know who they can reach out to during storms.
LDR is local body journalism co-funded by RNZ and NZ on Air

title: Warnings issued as heavy rain heads to Bay of Plenty, Northland
text:
Warnings issued as heavy rain heads to Bay of Plenty, Northland
MetService is forecasting heavy rain for Northland and eastern Bay of Plenty as a front moves eastward across northern and central North Island on Sunday and early Monday.
An orange rain warning is in place for the ranges of eastern Bay of Plenty. MetService forecasts 70 to 90mm of rain, peaking at 10 to 20mm/h expected. The warning is for 12 hours from 3pm Sunday to 3am Monday.

A yellow rain watch is in place for the north and east of Northland. MetService forecasts periods of heavy rain that may approach warning levels.
There was a low risk of localised downpours that could briefly boost rainfall rates to 25 to 40mm/h, it said, and a moderate chance of upgrading to a warning. The watch is until 8pm Sunday.

title: Camera captures sudden shift in weather as snow storm blows over Remutaka Ranges
text:
Camera captures sudden shift in weather as snow storm blows over Remutaka Ranges
A traffic camera has captured the dramatic shift in weather at the Remutaka Ranges as snow falls in the lower North Island and blankets the south.
A road snowfall warning was in place for the Remutaka Hill Rd until 2am Wednesday.
MetService's traffic camera at Remutaka Pass showed a sudden change from sunny, blue skies to frosty, gloomy conditions as a storm blew over the mountains.
Within the space of 15 minutes, clouds and snow covered the sky and even the camera.
MetService said snow showers between 2 and 4 cm could accumulate about the summit with lesser amounts to 300 metres.
Meteorologist Braydon White said cold southerly air was blowing its way up the country bringing chilly weather to the capital.
"We've seen some snow on the Remutaka road, generally down to about 300 metres. There have been some reports of some small hail around in the city, so it's definitely pretty cold."
He said the temperature dropped to 2 degrees in the region, low enough that some flurries made it to sea level in the central city.
White said it had been several years since snow had fallen in the city, and more could be on the way tonight.

title: Severe gales, thunderstorms possible as weather watches issued across country
text:
Strong wind and rain watches are in place for parts of the South Island and lower North Island as the weekend approaches.
MetService meteorologist John Law said "some wetter, windier weather" is moving back across Aotearoa on Thursday.
As it moved up, the western side of the South Island was as risk of thunderstorms.
By the end of Thursday, Law said the wet weather would make its way up to the North Island.
Along with the wet, there would be strong winds around areas including Canterbury high country and Wellington.
Friday would see "strong southerly winds for the south as well," Law said.
A heavy rain watch is in place for the Tararua Range from midnight Thursday until noon on Friday.
Periods of heavy rain were expected with the possibility of amounts approaching warning criteria.
MetService said there was a moderate change the watch would be upgraded to a warning.
Strong wind watches have been issued for Wellington, Canterbury high country, Christchurch, Banks Peninsula and the Canterbury Plains, coastal Otago and coastal Southland and southern Fiordland.
Wellington's watch was in place from 7pm Thursday until 2am Friday.
Canterbury high country's watch was already in place, and was due to end at 6pm.
The watch for Christchurch, Banks Peninsula and the Canterbury Plains is in place from 6pm to midnight Friday.
Coastal Otago's kicks in from noon Friday until 9pm, while the watch for coastal Southland and southern Fiordland is from 9am until 6pm Friday.
MetService said for all watches, winds could approach severe gales in exposed areas.
All watches had a moderate change of being upgraded to warnings.
"Those driving in gale-force winds are urged to take extra care, especially those operating high-sided vehicles, towing vehicles and motorcycles," MetService said.
The wet and windy weather follows chilling temperatures across the country.
In the South Island, the Mount Cook / Pukaki area registered a freezing -7C early on Monday morning.
Shortly after 7am, Twizel was still shivering at -7.5C, the MetService site recorded.
On Wednesday, MetService meteorologist Alwyn Bakker said a ridge of high pressure had gradually started to drift off to the east giving a bit of a lift in temperatures.
"Thursday is going to be a little bit warmer for most people, but then as we get into the weekend, it's going to start dipping down into those cooler temperatures again."

images.caption: Wet and windy weather is expected for New Zealand. Photo credit: Supplied / MetService

title: Questions asked after monsoon-like rains sweep Wellington
text:
Questions asked after monsoon-like rains sweep Wellington
Questions are being raised about the cause of flooding in parts of the capital.
Wellington residents reported torrents surging down Tinakori Road in Thorndon on Saturday morning and rising around parked cars, with some joking a boat or kayak lane was needed on the busy street.
MetService issued a Severe Thunderstorm Warning for Wellington for the morning, including for torrential rain, after thunderstorms were detected near the city and airport, moving east-northeast. The formal alert was extended during the morning, before later being lifted.
Wellingtonian Rebekah Ward described watching floodwaters rising towards the doors of shops in Tinakori Road, while having breakfast there.
She said the "river" of water rose to the bottom of parked cars and even knocked over a scooter, prompting fears her own vehicle could be swept away.
The timing of the downpour was an "ironic" reminder of the monsoon she would soon experience on a trip to India, Ward said.
"There were cars parked along Tinakori Road and the water was getting higher and higher and higher... and I could see that the water was getting up to the level of the bottom of the car door, and I was thinking 'oh gosh, am I going to have a car when this is finished?'
MetService meteorologist Paris Marshall said multiple reports and observations of hail and intense rainfall were logged across the capital on Saturday morning as the storm moved east toward Lower Hutt.
The intensity was at a level where flash flooding around streams, gullies and urban areas were possible, and instruments recorded 40 millimetres of rain in half an hour at MetService's Kelburn station, near Tinakori Road, Marshall said.
Fire and Emergency NZ said it had no weather-related callouts from the downpours.
Responding to commentary on social media, Wellington's deputy mayor Ben McNulty said three-water provider Tiaki Wai should investigate what went wrong, adding that the area had not flooded significantly during heavy rain events earlier in the year.
Tiaki Wai was approached for comment.
However, Tiaki Wai did issue an alert that heavy rain had lead to a discharge of fully treated wastewater into the Waiwhetū Stream, in Lower Hutt, which empties into Wellington Harbour.
This could make the water discharge appear cloudy or murky or mean it has an odour, they warned, and all recreational water users should follow Land Air Water Aotearoa (LAWA) advice and stay out of the stream the next two to three days.
The LAWA website had all swimming spots on the north and east of Wellington Harbour as well as Oriental Bay marked as unsuitable for swimming, on Saturday.
Snowfall warnings issued for high parts of the country, strong wind watch for Auckland
Elsewhere in the country, MetService issued snowfall warnings for the Desert Road (SH1) and Lewis Pass (SH7), while strong southwest winds prompted a yellow Strong Wind Watch for Auckland, through till 7pm Saturday.
Snow was expected to settle on Desert Road from late Saturday afternoon and into the evening, with 2 to 4cm possible near the summit and light flurries down to 800m.
Snow showers were possible on Lewis Pass on Saturday afternoon and evening with 1 to 2cm of snow accumulated.

title: Watch: 'Cloud burst' hits Grey District, flooding homes and causing a slip
text:
About half-a-dozen homes flooded in the South Island overnight.
Fire and Emergency (FENZ) crews responded to flooded homes in Greymouth, Cobden, Brunner and Runanga in the Grey District.
Southern shift manager Lyn Crosson said they also responded to a slip on the road in Cobden.
Crosson said they were gearing up for more heavy rain and possible flooding this afternoon.
Cobden resident Jonathan Stark says his rain gauge shows more than 120 millimetres of rain fell in about three hours overnight.
"It was pretty wild weather. It started about three o'clock with heavy rain and then thunderstorms as well. We had 45 minutes of a proper downpour," Stark said.
"Our weather station, we checked this morning and it said we had 129 mills of rain in under three hours.
"We thought the water would have disappeared overnight like it normally does, but we woke up this morning to get ready to go to work and found what we found."
Water was still halfway up the tyres of his ute.
His garage was also still under water and he expected his spa pool would also be ruined.
Stark expected the damage to his property could cost a couple of thousand dollars.
He had never seen anything like Friday morning's downpour in his five years on the West Coast.
"I've never seen nothing major like this," Stark said.
"I've seen rain - it rains on the West Coast, but nothing so quick and furious."
His cat remained trapped under the house as they could not access it with the water still surrounding the property, but he was pleased his cat had survived the downpour.
"I can hear the cat crying out to get help but we just can't get to it," Stark said.
Surrounding streets were under water.
"It just happened so quickly," he said.
Char Stevens said she was still trapped in her Cobden home.
"We can't go anywhere - that's for sure. We're stuck," she said.
"It's come down from the bonnets of the cars to the tyres now. We're raised so the house is all right but when I waded out before to get wood it was basically up to my knees."
Stevens was woken by thunder early this morning, but it was not until she got out of bed later on that she realised her street looked like a river and water was up to the bonnets of cars.
"All I heard at 3am was the massive thunderstorm," she said.
"I went back to sleep and then my flatmate, when I got up, was like 'come outside'. We opened the door and we couldn't go any further because the water was right up there.
"When it got a bit lighter we could see that it was fully flooded. It's still flooded now but it looks like it's slowly receding. It's just crazy."
More to come
A heavy rain watch had been in place for the Westland Ranges from 8pm on Thursday until 3am on Friday, with heavy rain forecast to move northwards over the North Island on Friday.
West Coast Emergency Management said on social media it was a "cloud burst style rain event".
"Please take care as first light arrives."
Images uploaded by Grey District Council showed surface flooding in Greymouth.
State Highway 7 was closed between Greymouth and Stillwater. The New Zealand Transport Agency advised road users to avoid the area or delay their journey if possible.
The council said parts of Wickes Street, Richmond Street, Bright Street, Barkley Place, Peel Street, and Sturge Street, all had high surface water, and there were reports of a tree down on Taylorville Road.
Heather Keats with details of this weekend’s cold snap
MetService head of weather Heather Keats told Morning Report the heavy rain would head up the west of the country over the next couple of days.
"Sunday's okay, but today and tomorrow, very much looking messy," she explained.
"We've got a bunch of fast-moving features and fronts tied up and that will be thunderstorms, snow, heavy rain, maybe even some small tornadoes and water spouts. And that'll race up and over the country - the North Island - tomorrow, and then it kind of races away.
"But then we're left with a very cold southerly flow. So we've got every type of weather coming over the next sort of 48 hours."
Localised clean-up
Grey District Mayor Tania Gibson said the rain had eased for the moment, but more showers were expected later in the day.
"Our crews have been out since two o'clock this morning, and now that we're in the light of day, there's a lot of assessment going on, there's a lot of debris to clear, there's still road closures in the area and we're trying to find out who's been affected the most.
"But... some of those outer-lying suburbs have been affected and we had a lot of rain come through on the catchment on the hills, which has brought a lot of rain down into town and to those areas and which has brought a lot of debris down as well."
She said there would be a reasonably significant clean-up ahead.
"I was at home, but I was up because we had some poor little lambs in the paddock outside that were crying their hearts out. So, but we do have rain events quite often, but it's hard to assess until you start getting the reports because sometimes, nothing happens, but when they happen in those isolated areas, it's very quick.
"But where I was there wasn't a lot, and driving into town this morning there wasn't a lot."

title: Tornadoes, cold snaps, heavy rain and some sun: 'Every type of weather' forecast this weekend
text:
Tornadoes, cold snaps, heavy rain and some sun: 'Every type of weather' forecast this weekend
Heather Keats with details of this weekend’s cold snap
Strong winds could close the Auckland Harbour Bridge this weekend, and a wintry blast of polar air set to bring snow, severe frost and icy conditions across parts of the country.
By Friday, weather watches and warnings were already in place for parts of both the North and South Island, including for snow on roads, strong winds and heavy rain.
A yellow Strong Wind Watch was in place for Auckland, with meteorologists warning Aucklanders could get gusts up to 100 kilometres per hour. NZTA said winds that strong could affect travel across the bridge for short periods.
The strong wind was expected to arrive Friday night, and strengthen into Saturday afternoon, before easing that night.
Motorists were asked to drive to the conditions and pay attention to electronic message boards on the motorway, which will advise if any lane closures and reduced speed limits are required.
About half-a-dozen homes flooded overnight between Thursday night and Friday morning in the Grey District, and there was a slip on a road on Cobden, with more heavy rain expected.
Weekend conditions will bring an icy blast, and could bring tornadoes
The heavy rain and strong winds could spark tornadoes in the North Island, MetService head of weather Heather Keats told Morning Report on Friday morning.
It could be an 'inside' end to the week' - at least for Friday and Saturday, she agreed: "Sunday's okay, but today and tomorrow, very much looking messy".
"We've got a bunch of fast-moving features and fronts tied up and that will be thunderstorms, snow, heavy rain, maybe even some small tornadoes and water spouts. And that'll race up and over the country - the North Island - tomorrow, and then it kind of races away.
"But then we're left with a very cold southerly flow. So we've got every type of weather coming over the next sort of 48 hours."
Thunderstorms had already hit Westland and Fiordland overnight, she said, with about 250 lightning strikes.
"Nothing crazy, but that's just the start of it."
On Friday morning, heavy rain was hitting Buller and Nelson Lakes.
A yellow Heavy Rain Watch was in place till midnight Friday for the Tararua Ranges, north of Wellington, with a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning.
And more weather watches or warnings were likely to come, with tornadoes possibly in the mix, Keats said.
"The entire western coastline of New Zealand, I'm talking all the way up around Northland and the Coromandel Peninsula and then it'll track a little bit over to the eastern side as well.
"Thunderstorms, really strong wind gusts, and the conditions are right to see some water spouts and some small tornadoes. We don't say that lightly. Not all thunderstorms produce thunder, not all thunderstorms produce tornadoes. But we are seeing that signal in the models. So it's going to be a watch-this-space today.
"If you are anywhere sort of near those western coastlines, keep an eye on your app because if we do see a severe thunderstorm, we will put out that warning opportunity for you to get safe."
As for temperatures, among main centres Christchurch was likely to get bragging rights for the coldest, with it dipping below zero.
A Road Snowfall Warning was in place for the Desert Road, SH1, and snow was likely for Ruapehu, Keats said. While eight South Island roads had Road Snowfall Warnings in place, including Lewis Pass, Arthur's Pass, Porters Pass, Lindis Pass and Haast Pass.
Snow was also expected on the SH1 Dunedin to Waitati Highway.
Sunshine expected back for Sunday
"Because it's fast-moving, [the windy weather] won't be hanging around for long," Keats said.
"Once it clears out on Sunday, and we will have sun, we will have some nice weather coming for most of the country on Sunday, it just drops to be freezing. So we're talking -4C for Christchurch.
"We're talking pretty average temperatures for places like Auckland - so high of 14C, low of 4C, but with that wind chill, it's going to feel closer to 1C.

title: Elusive fogbow photographed at Cobar, western NSW
text:
- A fogbow has been seen at Cobar, NSW, much to the delight of an amateur photographer.
- Fogbows are similar to rainbows, but are generated by much smaller moisture droplets.
- The conditions in western NSW generally do not permit the phenomenon, which is more common in parts of the Northern Hemisphere.
There was no pot of gold at its end, but the appearance of a rare optical phenomenon allowed amateur photographer Marie Johnson to capture an image she will always treasure.
The Cobar resident could not believe her luck when she spotted a white, fuzzy bow stretching across her western New South Wales property last week.
"I've never seen one. Never, ever seen one in my life," Johnson said.
"This is just sitting right on our farm; it was amazing.
"I've wanted to get some photos of the fog in the background with the old house and … when I turned around, I went, 'Oh my God, look at that.'"
At first she thought she had snapped a "big white rainbow".
"That's why I took the photos and put them up [on social media]," she said.
"Then a few other people came on and travellers, [and I learned] it's called a fogbow.
"I just thought, 'Oh wow, that's amazing.'"
Johnson said the fogbow faded away after about half an hour.
Rainbow's elusive cousin
Bureau of Meteorology senior meteorologist Jonathan Howe said fogbows were made up of fog droplets, which could be 1000 times smaller than the rain droplets that generated rainbows.
He said fogbows were uncommon in Australia.
"We often see pictures of fog growth from Canada, Europe, northern Asia and that's because of their position relative to the equator," Howe said.
Howe said fogbows were unusual in warmer, drier areas such as western NSW.
"Quite critically, it needs to be fog because mist droplets are quite large," he said.
"Fog in western NSW is probably not as common as the eastern parts of the state. So to see this at Cobar is quite impressive.
"They are more likely in southern parts of the country and particularly in winter, and that's because the sun is a little bit lower on the horizon."
Even more unusual are lunar fogbows, which occur at night.
"They are incredibly rare," Howe said.
"The moon needs to be at a very certain angle, and there needs to be … no clouds in the sky."
- ABC
